query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A computationally designed surface coating, with optimized composition to favor the in situ formation of a protective, slow-growing oxide (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3), will enhance the oxidation resistance of refractory high-temperature alloys compared to untreated or conventionally coated samples.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-temperature alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW RHEA) that forms non-protective or rapidly growing oxides during high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Apply a coating whose composition is optimized via density functional theory (DFT) and thermodynamic modeling to establish the ideal oxidation free energies and diffusion properties that promote the formation of a protective oxide scale.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidative environments (e.g., exposures around 1000–1430 °C in air or controlled oxidizing atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a slow-growing, adherent oxide layer (preferably Al2O3 or Cr2O3) on the coated surface, which acts as an effective diffusion barrier to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The optimized coating diffuses selected elements into the substrate upon high-temperature treatment, thereby generating a continuous protective oxide scale. This scale limits further oxygen ingress, retarding oxidation kinetics and reducing weight gain in service.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will display a reduced oxidation rate and a more stable, adherent protective oxide layer compared to both the untreated alloy and samples coated via conventional methods (e.g., the Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating produced by a fused slurry method).
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-temperature alloys or those treated with standard, non-optimized silicide coatings.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected primarily under conditions where high-temperature diffusion and oxidation kinetics are active; the protective effect may diminish if the operating temperature or environmental conditions fall outside the modeled regime.
generation.uncertainty: Precise optimal coating compositions, kinetics of oxide scale growth, and the full range of high-temperature operational conditions require further experimental validation and may vary with substrate composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of refractory high-temperature alloy samples: (1) untreated, (2) coated with a conventional Si-based silicide using a fused slurry method, and (3) coated with the computationally designed optimized coating. Expose all samples to the same high-temperature oxidative conditions (e.g., 1430 °C in a controlled atmosphere for a fixed duration). Characterize the surface and cross-sectional microstructures using XRD, SEM, and EDS, and perform thermogravimetric analysis to track oxidation kinetics.
measurements: Phase composition of the oxide scale via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the computationally optimized coating do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate or fail to develop a continuous, protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale compared to both the untreated and conventionally coated samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. decision.trend: Earlier efforts sought to overcome the poor high‐temperature oxidation resistance of refractory and high-temperature alloys by modifying the surface rather than relying solely on standard alloying. Initial studies using unmodified surfaces showed the formation of non‐protective oxides. This led to work such as that in PMC7475834, where a Si‐20Cr‐20Fe silicide coating was applied using a fused slurry method and high‐temperature treatment. The coating deliberately diffuses silicon into the substrate to create an outer layer that, upon oxidation at elevated temperatures, forms slow-growing SiO2 (among other mixed oxides) that acts as a barrier. While such coatings improved oxidation resistance, the evolution of the microstructure and the exact mechanistic understanding of how the protective oxide scales form and persist remain areas of active inquiry.
decision.unsolved: Although applying silicide coatings has proven effective, there remains an incomplete predictive understanding of the thermodynamic and kinetic factors that govern the formation of the desired protective, slow-growing oxide scales (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3). Specifically, determining the optimal coating composition and processing parameters to reliably produce such scales under varying high-temperature oxidative conditions is unsolved.
decision.lever: Develop a computational screening framework that uses density functional theory (DFT) and thermodynamic modeling to calculate oxidation free energies and predict phase stability of candidate coatings. Key parameters would include oxidation potentials that favor the formation of protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales, coating element diffusivities, and interfacial energies.
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the established trend of using surface coatings for oxidation resistance but addresses the remaining gap by quantitatively predicting optimal coating compositions and processing conditions. It thus leverages computational insight to overcome uncertainties in the oxidation mechanism revealed by experimental coatings, guiding the design of next-generation protective surfaces.
